headline: Recommended approving amended ordinances on pay-to-play rules for city grants and on protecting private significant trees during construction.
summary: Chair Scott's changes would require disclosure of certain nonprofit board political contributions instead of exempting them, so Community Preservation Act grants could still proceed. For tree protection, the usual fence radius is one foot for every inch of a tree's diameter. A significant tree has a minimum diameter of eight inches.

Recommended approving the amended ordinance to protect private significant trees during construction, 5-0.

Wednesday, November 18, 2026

6:00 PM

- Ward Two City Councilor Jefferson Thomas (J.T.) Scott

2. Mayor's Request Requesting ordainment of an amendment to Chapter 15, Article III of the (ID # 26-1408 ) Code of Ordinances.

Chair Scott reviewed his proposed amendments in the attachment,

Legislative Matters - 2026-11-18 Amending Ch. 15 Art. III Pay to Play (with

26-1408). He noted that the previously proposed change to the definition of financial assistance in Section 15-71, which would have exempted grants

- authorized by multi-member bodies, had been removed and that Section

**15-77** had been added to establish a waiver provision. Assistant City Attorney Jason Piques explained that both Chair Scott's proposed amendments and the previous version of the ordinance were legally sound and that the distinction was a matter of policy. In response to a question from Councilor Ewen-Campen, Chair Scott clarified that his proposed amendments would allow Community Preservation Act (CPA) grants to proceed even when a nonprofit board member had made a political contribution that could otherwise create a conflict. Rather than exempting these contributions entirely, the proposed amendments would require disclosure of the contribution, as outlined in Section 15-77. Councilor Strezo asked about the process for bringing the amendments before the City Council, and Chair Scott anticipated that the matter would likely be handled in a single meeting, with a vote that evening rather than being referred to committee. Councilor Strezo expressed concern that the proposed process could create additional red tape and bureaucracy. Councilor Mbah asked for clarification on the addition of a four calendar year lookback period in Section 15-72(e)(5). Assistant City Attorney Piques explained that the ordinance already includes lookback periods for applications for contracts and financial assistance, as well as a four year look forward period. The proposed language would help inform the review of new no-bid contracts or grants. He clarified that the disclosure would be part of the application process but would not prevent a grant from being approved. Councilor Davis added that if the intent of the amendments was to prevent elected officials from being influenced by campaign contributions, there could be concerns about having elected officials themselves responsible for granting waivers. Chair Scott acknowledged this as a valid point and reiterated that his intent was to ensure transparency through public disclosure. Councilor Ewen-Campen noted that contributions made by board members are considered collectively, meaning that contributions totaling $500 could be reached relatively easily by larger boards, even if individual contributions were small. Councilor Davis suggested that the threshold could be revisited through a future amendment. Councilor Ewen-Campen also raised concerns that it could be uncomfortable for the City Council to determine whether contributions were made in good faith. Councilor Davis reminded the Committee that the City is undertaking a comprehensive review of its ordinances, so there will be additional opportunities to identify and recommend further improvements to the ordinance as part of that process.

At the October 27, 2027 Legislative Matters Committee, Councilor Davis moved to strike “in their capacity” from Section 15-73(b), so the language would read “while serving as.” The motion was adopted on a roll call vote of 4 in favor (Councilors Davis, Mbah, Strezo and Scott), none opposed, one recused (Councilor Ewen-Campen) and one absent .

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE APPROVED AS

AMENDED

AYE:

- Ward Six City Councilor Davis, City Councilor At Large
- Mbah, Ward Three City Councilor Ewen-Campen, City
- Councilor At Large Strezo and Ward Two City Councilor
- Scott

3. Ordinance

By Councilor Sait

(ID # 26-1476 ) That Section 12-111.1 of the Code of Ordinances be amended as detailed

herein to protect private significant trees during construction.

Chair Scott introduced the attachment, Legislative Matters - 2026-11-18

Amending Sec. 12-111.1 Protection of Private Significant Trees , and

- reviewed the proposed amendment. Dr. Vanessa Boukili, Senior Urban

Forestry and Landscape Planner, explained that the change clarifies that the protection requirement does not apply to every tree on or abutting a lot, but rather to trees in the area surrounding construction.

- In response to questions from Councilor Davis about industry-standard tree

protection measures, Planner Boukili explained that these typically include installing a chain-link or similar fence around the tree, with a radius of one foot for every inch of the tree's diameter. She noted that requirements would be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, but this would serve as the general

standard. While different tree species have varying tolerances for root pruning, this standard should protect the tree's structural roots and allow it to recover from any necessary pruning. Planner Boukili added that a significant

- tree is defined as having a minimum diameter of eight inches.

Councilor Strezo asked about the review timeline outlined in Section B(2).

- Planner Boukili explained that the language was intentionally left flexible
- because the department does not have the capacity to review every permit.

- However, if a project is flagged or the department is made aware of a

potential concern, the provision allows them to require a review of the plan or amendment. While there is no specified timeline, the department would

aim to act quickly to protect the tree. They review all Green Score applications within two weeks and additional documents within one week, so a similar timeline could be expected.

- Councilor Ewen-Campen asked what would take precedence if construction

needed to occur directly along a property line. Planner Boukili explained that state law also provides protections for trees, including provisions that allow property owners to trim branches extending over their property but

prohibit actions that would effectively kill or seriously damage a tree, such as cutting off all of its roots on one side. Chair Scott added that projects

involving tree removal already require a separate tree removal permit, so the amendment would likely not add significantly to Planner Boukili's workload.

- Planner Boukili agreed. Chair Scott also raised concerns that the required
- fencing radius for larger trees could pose challenges on smaller lots. Planner

- Boukili noted that a building permit could still be issued, but the property

owner would separately need to obtain a tree removal permit, which would require a payment to the City. Neighbors whose trees are damaged may also

- have recourse under state law.

- In response to a question from Councilor Mbah, Planner Boukili noted that

the Tree Warden is working on a guidebook outlining tree protection measures.

Chair Scott moved to adopt the language in the handout Legislative

Matters - 2026-11-18 Amending Sec. 12-111.1 Protection of private significant trees

The motion was adopted on a roll call vote of 5 in favor (Councilors Davis, Mbah, Ewen-Campen, Strezo and Scott), none opposed and none absent.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE APPROVED AS

AMENDED

AYE:
